young.html: For parents: Mourning Becomes Electra is a long tragedy about a family destroyed by murder and revenge, written for adults. This path introduces the idea behind it; the full lesson is for older teens and adults.
Eugene O'Neill was America's first great playwright. He loved the old Greek tragedies, and he wondered: what if one of those ancient stories happened in an American family?

So he took a famous Greek story, about a king coming home from war and the trouble in his family, and moved it to a big white house in New England just after the American Civil War. The characters wear 1860s clothes and speak like Americans, but the old story's pattern of anger and revenge plays out again.

young.html: Old story, new place. Pick a fairy tale you know well, like Cinderella or the Three Little Pigs. Retell it as if it happened in your own town this year. Who would each character be? What would change, and what would stay the same?

full.html: Eugene O'Neill (1888–1953), the son of a famous touring actor, grew up in hotels and theaters, went to sea as a young man, and began writing plays after a long illness. His plays brought serious tragedy to the American stage. He won the Pulitzer Prize four times and, in 1936, the Nobel Prize in Literature, the only American playwright so honored. Mourning Becomes Electra, a trilogy of three plays, opened in New York in 1931 and ran about six hours with a dinner break.
About quotations: the play was first published in 1931 and is still under copyright, so this lesson describes it in our own words. See "Read the full text" above for where to find it.

O'Neill followed the plan of Aeschylus' Oresteia, earlier on this ladder, scene by scene, but replaced the gods and the curse of fate with the inner forces of a modern family: jealousy, guilt and hidden longings, as the psychology of his day described them.

items: Homecoming (Agamemnon). In 1865, General Ezra Mannon returns from the Civil War. His wife Christine, who hates him and loves another man, Captain Adam Brant, poisons him. Their daughter Lavinia, devoted to her father, discovers what her mother has done.

The Hunted (The Libation Bearers). Lavinia's brother Orin comes home wounded from the war. Lavinia convinces him of their mother's guilt, and together they take revenge on Brant. Christine, in despair, takes her own life.

The Haunted (The Eumenides). Lavinia and Orin travel to the South Seas and return changed. Orin, tormented by guilt, also dies. Lavinia, the last Mannon, refuses any escape: she orders the shutters nailed closed and shuts herself inside the house with the dead, to punish herself for the rest of her life.

full.html: In the Oresteia, the chain of revenge is finally broken by a court and the gods' mercy. In O'Neill's version there are no gods and no court, and the chain ends only when the last Mannon locks herself away. The modern tragedy has no Athens to rescue it.

The title plays on two meanings of "becomes": mourning "suits" Electra, as black clothes might, and Electra herself "becomes" mourning, turning into grief. The Mannons' house, with its white columns like a Greek temple's front, is O'Neill's stage image of a classical tragedy in an American setting.
Thinking O'Neill simply copied Aeschylus. He kept the plot's shape but changed its meaning: fate becomes psychology, and the gods' justice becomes a family's private punishment.

items: Aeschylus' Oresteia is the model, act by act.
Freud, in this era's volumes, gave O'Neill the language of hidden family feelings he used instead of the gods.
Euripides' Electra and Sophocles' Electra told the same story in different ways; O'Neill's title points to all of them.
Ibsen brought tragedy into a middle-class home; O'Neill made it American.
Is revenge ever justice? What breaks a chain of revenge?
Can a family's past trap its children? How can people escape it?
What changes when a story about gods becomes a story about psychology?
Why do old myths keep being retold?

questions: Why do you think O'Neill moved a Greek story to America after the Civil War?
In the Greek version, a court ends the revenge. What could have ended it for the Mannons?
Lavinia chooses to punish herself. Is that brave, or sad, or both?
What stories have you seen retold in a new time or place?
How do families pass down feelings, good and bad, without meaning to?
care: A tragedy of murder, revenge and suicide within a family, for adult readers. The lesson summarizes the plot without detail.
